Let’s step back in time for a moment— way back—into Chapter 2: How Early Humans Lived and Loved.
Imagine a world with no fences, no mortgages, and no wedding vows tying anyone down. For tens of thousands of years, people wandered through forests and grasslands, moving together in small groups. They gathered food, raised their kids, and faced whatever the wild threw at them—always side by side.
In these tight-knit bands, everyone leaned on each other. Not just for the basics, like food and shelter, but for comfort, laughter, and that sense of connection we all crave. The lines between “mine” and “yours” were pretty fuzzy. Food was shared, children were cared for by lots of different adults, and relationships blended into daily life almost seamlessly.
The idea of one person “owning” another, or love being boxed into a lifelong partnership? That would've sounded strange to them. Instead, intimacy was often a community thing—with bonds forming, shifting, and evolving as people needed.
You can actually still catch glimpses of this in some modern hunter-gatherer societies. In these groups, it’s totally normal for people to have multiple lovers, sometimes even at the same time. Sure, jealousy pops up—but it’s not the jealous rage you might expect. The focus is on cooperation and harmony, because everyone knows their survival depends on strong social ties.
There’s a great story about a researcher who lived with a group deep in the rainforest. She noticed kids rarely knew exactly who their biological fathers were—and honestly, nobody seemed to mind. Uncles, friends, neighbors—everyone pitched in to help raise the kids. And when she asked about marriage, people just laughed and shrugged. “Why would anyone want to limit themselves to just one person?” one woman joked, like it was the punchline to a joke.
These aren’t just quirks from a handful of remote tribes. They’re windows into a way of life that shaped our instincts for generations upon generations. In a world where resources were unpredictable and dangers lurked everywhere, sharing—whether it was food, shelter, or affection—was simply the smart move. It built trust, cut down on conflict, and made sure no one was left out.
Of course, not every society worked exactly the same way. Some groups did start to develop stricter rules, especially as they grew larger or ran into new challenges. But for most of human history, people lived in ways that favored flexibility, generosity, and a kind of sexual openness that’s honestly tough to picture today.
Now, that doesn’t mean early humans were always searching for someone new, or that they didn’t form deep, meaningful bonds. Love, attachment, loyalty—they mattered then just as much as they do now. But these feelings existed right alongside a wider sense of connection. Intimacy could look a lot of different ways, and the well-being of the group was just as important as any one person’s desires.
So, when you find yourself wondering why monogamy can feel so complicated sometimes, it’s worth remembering this history. The longing for novelty, the spark of attraction, even the push and pull between commitment and desire—these aren’t signs that you’re failing. They’re echoes of a time when human sexuality was shaped by the needs of small, interdependent communities. And honestly, those needs are still humming quietly beneath the surface, even today.
